discovery: Metal-halide perovskite semiconductors for efficient solar cells
motivation: Metal-halide perovskites are a new class of solution-processed semiconductor. Their optoelectronic quality rivals that of crystalline silicon and gallium arsenide, and a whole field has grown from them within fifteen years. Miyasaka first used halide perovskites as photovoltaic absorbers (2009). Park and Snaith independently showed in 2012 that solid-state perovskite cells could work efficiently, and Snaith showed that the perovskite itself carries charge over long distances rather than acting only as a sensitizer. Their work showed that these materials combine sharp absorption edges, weakly bound excitons, long carrier diffusion lengths and unusual tolerance to defects. This physics was clarified by careful spectroscopy and has changed how we think about semiconductors that are soft and full of defects. Single-junction cells now exceed 26% efficiency, perovskite–silicon tandems exceed 33%, and the materials are moving into LEDs, detectors and industrial production. This is a fundamental physical discovery that changed what a field can make.
